output.headline: UK data watchdog’s children’s data ruling against TikTok stands as it resumes algorithm inquiry
output.standfirst: TikTok drops its appeal and will pay the UK watchdog, which fined the video app £12.7m for failing to enforce its minimum age limit of 13 and remove underage users
output.bodyHtml:
The UK’s data watchdog will receive a £12.7m fine from TikTok after the video app dropped its appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform.

Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.”

TikTok, which has more than 30 million users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation.

Chinese-owned TikTok said it had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”, though it still disagreed with the ruling.

The Information Commissioner’s Office punished the video app in 2023 for inadequate checks of who was using the platform and failing to remove underage users.

When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service.

The ICO said TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020. TikTok also failed to provide users with how their data was being collected and used, as well as neglecting to obtain parental consent.

At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts.

“Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said.

Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’s new under-16 age limit for accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year.

The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has warned that “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. The country’s eSafety commissioner has said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.
